record.context_brief: unique all-tiles tiling when a+b=1 mod 3
record.original_question: Let T113(a,b) count tilings of the (a,b)-benzel when both stone orientations are allowed and all three bone orientations are allowed. Whenever a+b is congruent to 1 modulo 3, is it true that T113(a,b) = 1, so that the region has exactly one tiling?

evidence.quote: For 0 <= i, j <= 1 and 0 <= k <= 3 we define Tijk (a, b) as the number of ways to tile the (a, b)-benzel if the set of allowed prototiles contains the right stone iff i = 1, contains the left stone iff j = 1, and contains k of the bones. We say that such a tiling is an i, j, k tiling.

Problem 14: Is it true that T113 = 1 when a+b is 1 (mod 3)? (Note that a + b equiv 1 is the situation in which the Conway-Lagarias invariant coincides with the area of the region being tiled, so that all the tiles must be right-pointing stones.)
Comment: This problem is resolved in the affirmative by Theorem 1.1 of [3].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the family of planar regions known as benzels, defined as follows. Working in the triangular grid in the plane, the (a,b)-benzel (for positive integers a,b) is a hexagonal-like region obtained by intersecting suitable half-planes; concretely it is composed of unit triangles and admits tilings by certain prototiles. The allowed prototiles are of two types:
 - Stones: small rhombic tiles of two chiralities, the "right stone" and the "left stone".
 - Bones: elongated tiles in three possible orientations.

For 0 ≤ i, j ≤ 1 and 0 ≤ k ≤ 3, let T_{ijk}(a,b) denote the number of tilings of the (a,b)-benzel in which the set of allowed prototiles contains the right stone if and only if i = 1, contains the left stone if and only if j = 1, and contains exactly k of the three bone orientations.

In particular, T_{113}(a,b) counts tilings of the (a,b)-benzel where both stone chiralities and all three bone orientations are permitted.

Prove or disprove: whenever a + b ≡ 1 (mod 3), one has T_{113}(a,b) = 1; that is, the (a,b)-benzel admits exactly one tiling, which necessarily uses only right-pointing stones (since in this congruence class the Conway–Lagarias invariant equals the area of the region).
artifact.status_search_result: The problem has been resolved affirmatively. A subsequent paper proves (as its Theorem 1.1) that when a+b ≡ 1 (mod 3), the (a,b)-benzel admits a unique tiling, consisting entirely of right-pointing stones. This corresponds to the case where the Conway–Lagarias invariant matches the region's area, forcing a unique tiling.
